justification: Round 2 is a genuine, verified fix of both round-1 technical majors, plus every round-1 minor, and I found no new factual errors. I formed my own judgement of the article first, then checked the round-1 files: (1) Headline timings: all timing programs now carry '#:property Optimize=true' (doubling, sorted-gap, hidden; the crossover program already had it), the Optimize=true directive is explained in prose where it first appears, and the opening hook now says 'a couple of seconds' rather than 'about nine seconds'. I re-ran the doubling program three times myself on this machine (dotnet run doubling.cs, SDK 10.0.401): 5,000 laps took 7-8 ms and 80,000 laps took 2.25-2.42 s, consistent with 'a couple of seconds' and with the article's own printed 7 ms / 2138 ms sample row. (2) The closest-pair hook is now resolved: a new id=sorted-gap program sorts the laps and scans adjacent gaps, asserts it agrees with the brute-force ClosestGap on a warm-up array, and times both at 40,000 and 80,000. I re-ran it twice myself: 40,000 laps went from 555-628 ms (quadratic) to 10.0-13.6 ms (sorted), 80,000 from 2154-2254 ms to 6.9-7.3 ms, match='yes' both times -- reproducing the article's printed 589/9.7 and 2158/8.1 rows and the 'a couple of hundred times faster' claim (2158/8.1 = 266x) within noise. Both fixes are real, not cosmetic: the reader now sees the payoff the opening promised, using the same Optimize=true build the article teaches elsewhere. Every round-1 minor is also fixed and I checked each is not just papered over: HashSet<T>.Add (not .Contains) is now the cited method, with the O(1)-below-capacity / O(n)-on-resize split I confirmed word-for-word against the live Microsoft Learn page, and the article now adds the 'expected' and 'amortized' qualifiers the brief requires; the growth-rate table now states it describes the pure function g(n), not every function in O(g(n)), and the n! row gets an exact derivation ((n+1)(n+2)...(2n), a product of n terms each > n, so the multiplier exceeds n^n) which I re-derived and confirms; the crossover section now names the actual extra constant (a fresh n-element buffer allocated once per MergeSort call, full-depth recursion to single elements, 7 recursive calls for n=8) instead of asserting it; the formal definition adds 'for non-negative f and g' and the 0 <= f(n) clause NIST states; a new paragraph adds little-o and the two Omega conventions (NIST/CLRS 'for every sufficiently large n' versus the weaker Hardy-Littlewood 'infinitely many n' convention), which I checked verbatim against the live NIST little-o page (for all c > 0 there exists k such that 0 <= f(n) < c*g(n) for all n >= k) -- an exact match to the article's wording; the toolchain line now reads '.NET 10 (SDK 10.0.401, runtime 10.0.12)', matching dotnet --version on this machine, and 'travels with it everywhere' is softened to 'roughly, on any machine, until cache effects or timer noise intrude'; docs/crosslinks/complexity/big-o-notation.md now exists and is sensible (eight planned links with anchor text, target route and location, plus a boundaries section that correctly scopes this article against sorting-algorithms-compared, analyzing-loops-and-recursion, binary-search, arrays-and-dynamic-arrays and hash-tables); and exercise solution 3 is reworded from a loose 'the sorting table showed the opposite outcome' to a literal statement of which class beat which ('insertion sort -- O(n^2), the larger class -- beat merge sort -- O(n log n)'). I re-derived every complexity claim on the page from scratch rather than trusting the prior round's derivations: the n(n-1)/2 pair count, the (c=4, n0=40) and (c=43, n0=1) witnesses for 3n+40, the not-O(n) proof for the pair search, the exercise witnesses (c=61, n0=1) and (c=3, n0=13) for 2n^2+9n+50, the Theta(n^2) sandwich (1/4, 1/2, n0=2), the true/false exercise (all six answers correct, including the 2^(2n) vs 2^n non-containment), the budget table (12! fits and 13! does not; 2^29 fits and 2^30 does not; n^2 limit exactly floor(sqrt(1e9)) = 31,622; n^3 limit exactly 1,000), and the doubling-sum nested-loop exercise (sum of powers of two below n is Theta(n), bounded in [n/2, 2n), and the printed steps/n column of 1.02-1.64 sits inside that band with the n=1,000,000 row matching my own hand calculation of 1,048,575 exactly). All of these check out with no arithmetic or logical errors. I also independently verified every primary source cited for a load-bearing claim by opening it this round: the NIST little-o definition (exact match); HashSet<T>.Add's O(1)/O(n) resize split (exact match); Sedgewick and Wayne 2.1's insertion-sort compares (~N^2/4 average, ~N^2/2 worst, N-1 best -- exact match); Sedgewick and Wayne 2.2's mergesort compares (between 1/2 N lg N and N lg N) and the 10-15 percent cutoff gain (exact match, and the article's own measured 80-91 percent of pure -- i.e. a 9-20 percent gain -- falls in the same order Sedgewick and Wayne report); and Array.Sort's introsort description (insertion sort at <=16 elements, heapsort past 2*log N partitions, quicksort otherwise, O(n log n) overall -- exact match). Against the two ranking pages I read this round, the article is clearly ahead on technical substance: Wikipedia has the definition and the o/Omega/Theta family but no runnable, verified code and no small-n crossover; GeeksforGeeks has a definition and per-class code snippets but no witness proofs, no measured timings, no Omega/Theta/little-o and no primary-source citations at all. This article has all of that plus its own worked witnesses, a verified small-n crossover with the real cause named, and every documented .NET operation's complexity stated with its qualifying condition. What keeps this at 9.0 rather than higher: (1) the claim that '#:property Optimize=true...asks the compiler for optimized code, the way a release build would' is only backed by the generic file-based-apps directive page (which documents #:property's syntax but not what the Optimize property itself does); the claim is well known, uncontroversial and is demonstrated empirically by the article's own before/after tables, but it has no dedicated citation the way every other non-obvious claim on the page does. (2) My own reruns of the doubling program showed more run-to-run variance than the article's stated 'every growth factor stayed between 3.9 and 4.5' -- one of my three runs hit x5.0 at 20,000 laps -- though this machine had heavy concurrent background load (Docker Desktop and other processes) during my checks, which plausibly explains it rather than the article being wrong; still, the stated range reads more precise than a shared machine can reliably deliver, and a hedge word ('typically', 'usually') would make it more robust. Neither issue is a factual error, a broken derivation or a source misquote, so neither caps the score, but they are the reason this is not a 9.5 or 10.

issues.location: 'The count predicts growth, not milliseconds', the sentence introducing #:property Optimize=true
issues.problem: The claim 'Optimize=true...asks the compiler for optimized code, the way a release build would' is cited only to the file-based-apps directive page, which documents the #:property syntax in general (with TargetFramework and PublishAot as its examples) but does not itself discuss the Optimize property or its release-vs-debug effect. The claim is true and is demonstrated empirically by the article's own optimized/unoptimized tables, but it lacks a dedicated primary source the way every other non-obvious claim on the page has one.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add one more source for the Optimize MSBuild property specifically (for example the 'Common MSBuild project properties' page on learn.microsoft.com, or the Roslyn compiler options page describing -optimize), or reword the sentence to point at the article's own before/after measurement as the evidence rather than asserting the release-build equivalence as an external fact.

issues.location: 'The count predicts growth, not milliseconds', 'Three runs gave 7 to 11 ms for 5,000 laps and 2.14 to 2.26 seconds for 80,000; ... From 20,000 laps up, every growth factor stayed between 3.9 and 4.5.'
issues.problem: Re-running the id=doubling program myself three times (dotnet run, Optimize=true, same machine class) reproduced the qualitative shape (roughly quadruples per doubling, low seconds at 80,000) but one run's 20,000-lap growth factor was x5.0, outside the article's stated 3.9-4.5 band, and one 80,000-lap total was 2.42 s, slightly above the stated 2.14-2.26 s band. This machine had heavy concurrent background load during my checks, which plausibly explains the extra variance rather than the article's own three runs being wrong, but the stated range reads more precise than a shared/loaded machine reliably delivers.
issues.fixLooksLike: Soften 'every growth factor stayed between 3.9 and 4.5' to something like 'every growth factor stayed close to 4, typically between 3.9 and 4.5' so an occasional outlier run does not contradict the stated claim.
